etymology: A compound of star and gazer, one who gazes fixedly. In the KJV it renders the Hebrew of Isaiah’s taunt-song — those who divided the heavens into signs and read fates in them; not a wondering skywatcher but an astrologer.
biblical_def: The stargazer of the Authorized Version is no innocent admirer of the night sky; he is an astrologer, a diviner who reads doom and fortune in the courses of the stars. The modern ear hears stargazer and pictures a poet or a boy with a telescope — a harmless dreamer. Scripture means a practitioner of a forbidden art. When the LORD mocks fallen Babylon He lines her wise men up together: “Let now the astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators, stand up, and save thee from these things that shall come upon thee” (Isa 47:13), and pronounces their doom in the next breath — “they shall be as stubble; the fire shall burn them” (Isa 47:14). The stars they consulted could not deliver them from the God who made the stars. The root sin is worship misdirected: Moses warned Israel lest, seeing “the sun, and the moon, and the stars, even all the host of heaven,” they “shouldest be driven to worship them, and serve them” (Deu 4:19). The LORD had set those lights to mark seasons, not to master men. So Jeremiah forbids the trembling of the heathen: “Learn not the way of the heathen, and be not dismayed at the signs of heaven” (Jer 10:2). Amos names the idolatry outright — the star of a false god borne in procession (Amo 5:26). The stargazer trusts the creature and forgets the Creator, and the fire finds him.
webster_summary: One who divines by the stars; an astrologer, not a mere admirer of the heavens.
webster_full: STARGAZER, an astrologer; one who reads or pretends to read the fates of men in the position and courses of the stars.
A compound of star and gaze, to look fixedly.
In the KJV it never means a harmless skywatcher, but a diviner of the forbidden Chaldean art.
Isaiah ranks the stargazers with astrologers and monthly prognosticators, and none could save Babylon (Isa 47:13).
Moses forbade Israel to be driven to worship the host of heaven (Deu 4:19).
scriptures: Thou art wearied in the multitude of thy counsels. Let now the astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators, stand up, and save thee from these things that shall come upon thee.
Deu 4:19

And lest thou lift up thine eyes unto heaven, and when thou seest the sun, and the moon, and the stars, even all the host of heaven, shouldest be driven to worship them, and serve them, which the LORD thy God hath divided unto all nations under the whole heaven.
Jer 10:2
Thus saith the LORD, Learn not the way of the heathen, and be not dismayed at the signs of heaven; for the heathen are dismayed at them.
Amo 5:26
But ye have borne the tabernacle of your Moloch and Chiun your images, the star of your god, which ye made to yourselves.
corruption_summary: The stargazer’s art is alive and well — it has only traded the Chaldean tower for the newspaper column and the phone app.
corruption_paragraphs: This is one word whose sin the modern world has not forgotten but rebranded. The stargazer of Isaiah has become the horoscope column, the birth-chart reading, the app that tells a soul what the planets have decreed for its love and money and health. Millions who would blush to call themselves idolaters cheerfully ask their sign, and order a day by a forecast drawn from the stars. It is the very thing the LORD condemned in Babylon — the attempt to read the future in the heavens and to steer a life by the creature rather than by the Creator’s revealed word. The art is old; only its packaging is new. And its promise is the same lie: that the stars govern what in truth the living God governs.

Against this the LORD’s verdict still stands: “Let now the astrologers, the stargazers… stand up, and save thee” (Isa 47:13) — and they cannot, for “the fire shall burn them” (Isa 47:14). To the trembling believer Jeremiah says, “Learn not the way of the heathen, and be not dismayed at the signs of heaven” (Jer 10:2). The Christian’s times are in his Father’s hand, not in the zodiac; the stars are His servants, hung to declare His glory, not to dictate a man’s fate. To consult them is to bow, however faintly, to the host of heaven that Moses forbade (Deu 4:19), and to forsake the counsel of the God who numbers the stars and calls them all by their names.
roots_summary: The word means an astrologer — a diviner by the stars, not a lover of the night sky.
roots_lines: Stargazer — a compound of star and gazer, one who gazes.
In the KJV it always means an astrologer of the forbidden Chaldean art.
It stands beside “astrologers” and “monthly prognosticators” in Isaiah’s taunt (Isa 47:13).
The root sin is worshipping the host of heaven instead of its Maker (Deu 4:19).
None of Babylon’s stargazers could deliver her from the fire (Isa 47:14).
usage: The KJV’s stargazer is no dreamer with a telescope but a diviner of fates by the stars.
Isaiah set the stargazers up to save Babylon, and they could not lift a hand against the flame.
Learn not the way of the heathen: the stars mark seasons, they do not rule souls.

etymology: From the Old French enchantement, from Latin incantare, “to sing or chant upon” — the spell was literally a song sung over a thing or a person. In the KJV it names sorcery and the muttered incantation, not delight.
biblical_def: An enchantment in the Authorized Version is a magic spell — the muttered charm, the incantation by which the sorcerer sought power over serpents, seasons, and souls. The word carries the very picture buried in its Latin root: something chanted upon, a song sung over a thing to bend it. The modern ear has softened all this to mean charm and delight — a place is “enchanting,” a child is “enchanted” — but Scripture means the black art itself. When Moses stood before Pharaoh, “the magicians of Egypt, they also did in like manner with their enchantments” (Exo 7:11), aping the works of God until they could ape no more. It is set flatly among the sins that provoked the LORD to cast Israel out, who “used divination and enchantments, and sold themselves to do evil in the sight of the LORD” (2Ki 17:17). The Preacher notes its emptiness with a proverb’s edge: “Surely the serpent will bite without enchantment” (Ecc 10:11) — the charm fails when it is most wanted. And here is the glory: against the covenant people the whole art is powerless. Balaam was hired to curse Israel and could not, for “there is no enchantment against Jacob, neither is there any divination against Israel” (Num 23:23). No spell binds the God who keeps His own. The sorcerer sings his song over the world; the LORD answers, “What hath God wrought!”
webster_summary: A magical charm or incantation; a spell chanted to gain power, not a delight.
webster_full: ENCHANTMENT, the act of producing effects by charms, spells, and incantations; sorcery; magic.
From Latin incantare, to chant or sing upon; the spell was a song sung over its object.
The KJV uses it of Egypt’s magicians and of forbidden sorcery, never of mere charm or delight.
Pharaoh’s magicians withstood Moses with their enchantments until they failed (Exo 7:11).
No enchantment prevails against the covenant people of God (Num 23:23).
scriptures: Surely there is no enchantment against Jacob, neither is there any divination against Israel: according to this time it shall be said of Jacob and of Israel, What hath God wrought!
Exo 7:11
Then Pharaoh also called the wise men and the sorcerers: now the magicians of Egypt, they also did in like manner with their enchantments.
Surely the serpent will bite without enchantment; and a babbler is no better.
And they caused their sons and their daughters to pass through the fire, and used divination and enchantments, and sold themselves to do evil in the sight of the LORD, to provoke him to anger.
corruption_summary: The modern ear hears “enchantment” and thinks of charm and wonder; the AV means sorcery and the muttered spell.
corruption_paragraphs: The honest drift here runs from the terrible to the pretty. Once an enchantment was a curse a witch chanted over a field; now it is a fairy-tale word for delight — an enchanting evening, an enchanted forest. The softening is so complete that a reader of Exo 7:11 may miss that the magicians of Egypt were doing something wicked and real, not something whimsical. The word was gelded of its danger by centuries of romance and story, until the very syllables that once named a capital crime became the language of the greeting card. Recover the older weight, and the Scriptures sharpen: enchantment is the attempt to seize by ritual and incantation what God has not given.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond that honest slide from sorcery to charm — though the old art itself is quietly courted again in the neo-pagan revival of spells and manifesting. The principle to recover is the powerlessness of every enchantment against the LORD’s people. Balaam, the ablest diviner of the age, was paid in full to curse Jacob and could not raise a word against him, for “there is no enchantment against Jacob” (Num 23:23). The serpent bites without a charm and the charm cannot stop the serpent (Ecc 10:11); the whole art is a babble that saves no one. Israel perished not because enchantments overpowered her but because she chose them and “sold themselves to do evil” (2Ki 17:17). The believer needs no counter-spell; he needs only the covenant God over whom no song is sung, and the confession that answers every sorcerer: “What hath God wrought!”
roots_summary: The word means a spell or incantation — a song chanted over a thing to bend it — not charm or delight.
roots_lines: Enchantment — from Latin incantare, “to chant upon.”
The spell was a song sung over its object; hence sorcery, not mere charm.
Egypt’s magicians withstood Moses with their enchantments (Exo 7:11).
It stands among the covenant-breaking sins that ruined Israel (2Ki 17:17).
No enchantment can prevail against the people God has blessed (Num 23:23).
usage: The KJV’s enchantment is a sorcerer’s spell, not the charm of an enchanting view.
Pharaoh’s magicians matched Moses with their enchantments until the finger of God undid them.
There is no enchantment against Jacob: no spell binds the God who keeps His own.

etymology: From Old English sōth, “truth,” and secgan, “to say” — literally “truth-saying.” The word survives from an age when sooth meant true; the soothsayer claimed to speak the truth of things to come.
biblical_def: Soothsaying in the Authorized Version is divination practised for gain — the false prophecy of the fortune-teller who claims to speak what is true of things to come. The old English word means simply “truth-saying,” and there lies its lie: the soothsayer sells as truth what he cannot know, and takes money for it. Scripture strips the mask cleanly. At Philippi “a certain damsel possessed with a spirit of divination met us, which brought her masters much gain by soothsaying” (Act 16:16). Note the two marks the Spirit sets down: the power was a demon, and the fruit was profit for her owners. Paul did not bargain or interpret; grieved, he “said to the spirit, I command thee in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her. And he came out the same hour” (Act 16:18) — and her masters raged, for their gain was gone. The sin is old in Israel’s indictment: the LORD forsook His people because “they be replenished from the east, and are soothsayers like the Philistines” (Isa 2:6), borrowing the diviner’s trade from the heathen. And it is among the abominations the LORD vows to abolish in the day He purges His people: “thou shalt have no more soothsayers” (Mic 5:12). The soothsayer trades on the future; but the future belongs to the God who alone declares the end from the beginning.
webster_summary: The practice of foretelling by divination, often for money; false truth-saying about things to come.
webster_full: SOOTHSAYING, the act or practice of foretelling events; divination; the pretended telling of truth about the future.
From Old English sōth, truth, and secgan, to say — “truth-saying.”
The KJV uses it of divination for gain, a demonic counterfeit of prophecy.
The damsel at Philippi brought her masters much gain by soothsaying (Act 16:16).
Israel sinned by becoming soothsayers like the Philistines (Isa 2:6).
scriptures: And it came to pass, as we went to prayer, a certain damsel possessed with a spirit of divination met us, which brought her masters much gain by soothsaying:
And this did she many days. But Paul, being grieved, turned and said to the spirit, I command thee in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her. And he came out the same hour.
Isa 2:6

Therefore thou hast forsaken thy people the house of Jacob, because they be replenished from the east, and are soothsayers like the Philistines, and they please themselves in the children of strangers.
Mic 5:12
And I will cut off witchcrafts out of thine hand; and thou shalt have no more soothsayers:
corruption_summary: The word “sooth” for truth has died, but the trade of the soothsayer has only changed its shopfront.
corruption_paragraphs: The honest drift lies in the first half of the word. Sooth once meant truth — we keep a fossil of it in “forsooth” — and a soothsayer was one who claimed to tell the truth of what was coming. That claim is the whole fraud, and the modern reader, to whom “sooth” means nothing, may miss the irony that the Bible files the truth-teller among the liars. The practice is not archaic at all; only the label has faded. The psychic hotline, the tarot table, the palm-reader who takes a fee, the medium who charges by the hour — these are the damsel of Philippi and her masters, gain and a spirit both.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the sin is simply renamed, not reinterpreted. The principle to recover is where true knowledge of the future lies. The LORD alone “declares the end from the beginning,” and He gave His people prophets, not soothsayers, and now His completed Word. Paul’s answer to the spirit of divination was not a better prediction but a command: “I command thee in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her” (Act 16:18). Where Christ is named in power, the counterfeit falls silent and its profit dries up — which is exactly why the girl’s masters were enraged. Israel’s ruin began when she chose to be “soothsayers like the Philistines” (Isa 2:6), and her healing is promised in the same terms: “thou shalt have no more soothsayers” (Mic 5:12). A soul that trusts the LORD needs no fortune sold to it; its times are already kept in a faithful hand.
roots_summary: The word means divination for gain — false truth-telling about the future — not any innocent forecast.
roots_lines: Soothsaying — from sōth (truth) and secgan (to say), “truth-saying.”
The soothsayer claimed to speak the truth of things to come — and lied for money.
The damsel at Philippi brought her masters much gain by it (Act 16:16).
Its power was a demon, cast out at the name of Jesus Christ (Act 16:18).
The LORD vows to leave His purified people no more soothsayers (Mic 5:12).
usage: The KJV’s soothsaying is divination sold for a fee, not a weatherman’s honest guess.
Her masters loved her soothsaying for the gain it brought — until Paul silenced the spirit.
Israel became soothsayers like the Philistines, and the LORD forsook the house of Jacob.

etymology: From the Greek exorkistēs, from exorkizō, “to adjure, to bind by an oath” — from ex (out) and horkos (an oath). The exorcist bound spirits by a solemn adjuration, a formula sworn over them.
biblical_def: An exorcist in the Authorized Version is one who adjures evil spirits — who tries to drive them out by a sworn formula, a set of powerful names pronounced over the possessed. The Greek root is an oath: to exorcise is to put under oath, to bind a spirit by adjuration. The one place the word appears in the KJV is a warning, not a warrant. “Certain of the vagabond Jews, exorcists, took upon them to call over them which had evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth” (Act 19:13). Seven sons of Sceva tried it — the name of Jesus used as a technique, borrowed like a spell, spoken by men who did not belong to Him. The demon was not deceived: “Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye?” (Act 19:15). Then the possessed man “leaped on them, and overcame them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded” (Act 19:16). Here is the whole doctrine in one bruising scene: power over the powers of darkness is not in a formula but in a Person, and He is not on loan. The name of Jesus is not a charm to be conjured with; it is the confession of those He owns. Paul cast out devils because Christ dwelt in him; Sceva’s sons only chanted, and were stripped and beaten for their presumption.
webster_summary: One who claims to expel evil spirits by adjuration or formula; in Scripture, a counterfeit exposed at Ephesus.
webster_full: EXORCIST, one who pretends to expel evil spirits by conjuration, prayers, and ceremonies; one who adjures.
From Greek exorkizō, to adjure or bind by oath, from horkos, an oath.
The exorcist bound a spirit by a sworn formula of names pronounced over it.
The vagabond-Jewish exorcists borrowed the name of Jesus as a technique (Act 19:13).
The seven sons of Sceva were overpowered and fled naked and wounded (Act 19:16).
scriptures: Then certain of the vagabond Jews, exorcists, took upon them to call over them which had evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth.
And there were seven sons of one Sceva, a Jew, and chief of the priests, which did so.
And the evil spirit answered and said, Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye?
And the man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, and overcame them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded.
corruption_summary: The one biblical exorcist is a cautionary figure, not a model; his power was borrowed and it failed.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern imagination, fed on film and horror, pictures the exorcist as a heroic ritualist wielding holy water and Latin against a snarling demon. The Authorized Version’s single use of the word points the opposite way: to the vagabond sons of Sceva, who treated the name of Jesus as a formula they could work without knowing the One who bears it. The honest drift is toward sensationalism — the exorcist as spectacle — and it obscures the lesson. Scripture is not interested in technique; it is interested in whose you are. The demon answered the incantation with a question that unmasked the whole trade: “who are ye?” (Act 19:15).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond that drift into spectacle. The principle to recover is that authority over evil spirits is not a method but a Master. Sceva’s sons had the right name and the wrong standing; they adjured “by Jesus whom Paul preacheth” (Act 19:13) as men quoting another’s password, and the powers of hell were not fooled. Christ’s own cast out devils by His indwelling Spirit and His finished work, not by an approved rite; and even they were told to rejoice less that the spirits were subject to them than that their names were written in heaven. The believer does not conjure with the name of Jesus; he belongs to Him, and that belonging — not any borrowed formula — is the whole of his safety. The story ends with the exorcists fleeing naked and wounded (Act 19:16), and with the name of the Lord Jesus magnified, and many burning their books of curious arts. Power is in the Person, never in the technique.
roots_summary: The word means one who adjures evil spirits by a sworn formula — and at Ephesus it names a failed counterfeit.
roots_lines: Exorcist — from Greek exorkizō, “to adjure, to bind by oath.”
To exorcise is to put a spirit under oath by a formula of names.
The KJV’s only exorcists are the vagabond Jews who borrowed Christ’s name (Act 19:13).
The demon knew Jesus and Paul, but not the pretenders — “who are ye?” (Act 19:15).
Power over evil spirits lies in the Person of Christ, not in a technique (Act 19:16).
usage: The KJV’s exorcist is no hero but Sceva’s son, chanting a name that was not his to wield.
They adjured the spirit by Jesus whom Paul preacheth, and the spirit asked, “who are ye?”
The exorcists fled naked and wounded: the name of Jesus is a confession, not a charm.

etymology: A rendering of the Greek archisynagōgos, from archē (chief) and synagōgē (assembly, synagogue). Not a magistrate or prince but the presiding officer of a congregation — the man charged with the order of its worship.
biblical_def: The ruler of the synagogue in the Authorized Version is a congregational officer, not a civil prince. The word ruler misleads the modern reader, who hears in it a king or a governor; but this ruler ruled a house of worship, presiding over the reading of the Law, keeping the order of the assembly, appointing who should speak. He was a churchwarden of the old covenant more than a lord. So Jairus, “one of the rulers of the synagogue” (Mar 5:22), for all his office falls at the feet of Jesus and begs for a dying daughter — a ruler bowed before the Ruler of all. The office could serve Christ or oppose Him, and Scripture shows both. One ruler “answered with indignation, because that Jesus had healed on the sabbath day” (Luk 13:14), guarding a rule and missing the Lord of the sabbath standing before him. Another, Crispus, “the chief ruler of the synagogue, believed on the Lord with all his house” (Act 18:8), and his whole family with him. And it was the rulers of the synagogue at Antioch who, after the reading, “sent unto them, saying… if ye have any word of exhortation for the people, say on” (Act 13:15), opening the door for Paul’s great sermon. The office was ordinary; the question was always whether the man who held it would kneel to Christ or contend against Him.
webster_summary: The presiding officer of a Jewish synagogue, charged with the order of its worship — not a civil ruler.
webster_full: RULER OF THE SYNAGOGUE, the officer who presided over a Jewish assembly and directed its worship and the reading of the law.
From Greek archisynagōgos, “chief of the synagogue.”
He kept order, appointed readers and speakers, and governed the congregation — not the city.
Jairus, a ruler of the synagogue, fell at the feet of Jesus for his daughter (Mar 5:22).
Crispus, the chief ruler, believed on the Lord with all his house (Act 18:8).
scriptures: Mar 5:22
And, behold, there cometh one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name; and when he saw him, he fell at his feet,

And the ruler of the synagogue answered with indignation, because that Jesus had healed on the sabbath day, and said unto the people, There are six days in which men ought to work: in them therefore come and be healed, and not on the sabbath day.
Act 18:8
And Crispus, the chief ruler of the synagogue, believed on the Lord with all his house; and many of the Corinthians hearing believed, and were baptized.
And after the reading of the law and the prophets the rulers of the synagogue sent unto them, saying, Ye men and brethren, if ye have any word of exhortation for the people, say on.
corruption_summary: The word “ruler” tempts the reader to imagine a prince; the AV means the presiding officer of a congregation.
corruption_paragraphs: The honest difficulty is the word ruler. To the modern ear it names authority in the state — a monarch, a governor, a man over cities. The ruler of the synagogue governed no city; he governed a worship service. He was the officer who saw to the order of the assembly, chose the readers, and kept the peace of the congregation, closer to an elder or a warden than to a king. Read him as a civil ruler and Jairus’ humility loses its edge, for the wonder is precisely that a man of settled religious standing fell at the feet of an itinerant teacher and begged.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the drift is simply the widening of the word “ruler” in modern ears. The principle to recover is that office is no shield from the claims of Christ. The synagogue rulers stand in Scripture as a divided company: one indignant that Jesus healed on the sabbath, defending his rule against the Lord of the sabbath (Luk 13:14); another, Crispus, believing with all his house (Act 18:8); the rulers at Antioch unwittingly handing Paul the pulpit (Act 13:15); Jairus on his face pleading for his child (Mar 5:22). The lesson for any man in sacred office is plain. To preside over worship is not to be right with God; the same seat that Crispus filled in faith another filled in hardness. Rank in the visible church saves no one; the ruler of the synagogue, like the least of his flock, must himself fall at the feet of Jesus.
roots_summary: The word means the presiding officer of a synagogue — a warden of worship, not a civil prince.
roots_lines: Ruler of the synagogue — from Greek archisynagōgos, “chief of the synagogue.”
He presided over worship and the reading of the law, not over any city.
Jairus held the office and yet fell at the feet of Jesus (Mar 5:22).
One such ruler resented a sabbath healing and rebuked the people (Luk 13:14).
Crispus, the chief ruler, believed with all his house (Act 18:8).
usage: The KJV’s ruler of the synagogue is a warden of worship, not a governor of men.
Jairus was a ruler of the synagogue, and the ruler fell at the feet of the true Ruler.
Crispus the chief ruler believed, while another ruler fumed that Christ had healed on the sabbath.

etymology: From Old English mot, “a particle of dust,” the tiniest fleck the eye can catch. Unrelated to the modern moat, with which the ear now confuses it; the KJV means a speck or a splinter, not a ditch of water.
biblical_def: A mote in the Authorized Version is a tiny speck — a fleck of dust or splinter of chaff, the smallest thing that can lodge in an eye. The Lord chose it for the least of faults, setting it against a beam — a great baulk of timber — to expose the hypocrisy of the fault-finder. “Why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother’s eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?” (Mat 7:3). The whole force of the saying hangs on the disproportion: a speck in another’s eye scrutinized, a plank in one’s own ignored. The censorious man is quick to offer surgery — “Let me pull out the mote out of thine eye” (Mat 7:4) — while blind and impaled himself. The remedy is not to stop caring about the brother’s speck but to deal first with one’s own timber: “Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother’s eye” (Mat 7:5). Luke sets down the same searching word (Luk 6:41). Note that the mote is real — the brother does have a speck, and it ought to come out — but only a healed eye can heal another. The order is everything: self-judgment first, then brotherly help; repentance in me before correction of you. He who forgets the order is not zealous for holiness but a hypocrite peering past his own plank.
webster_summary: A tiny particle of dust or chaff; the smallest speck, set by Christ against a great beam.
webster_full: MOTE, a small particle; anything proverbially little; a speck of dust or a splinter, especially in the eye.
From Old English mot, a particle of dust; not to be confused with moat, a ditch.
The KJV uses it for the least of faults, set against the beam of one’s own great sin.
Christ asks why we behold the mote in a brother’s eye and not the beam in our own (Mat 7:3).
The healed eye alone can cast the mote from a brother (Mat 7:5).
scriptures: Mat 7:3
And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?
Mat 7:4
Or how wilt thou say to thy brother, Let me pull out the mote out of thine eye; and, behold, a beam is in thine own eye?
Mat 7:5
Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye.
Luk 6:41
And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but perceivest not the beam that is in thine own eye?
corruption_summary: The modern ear half-hears “moat” and loses the picture; the AV means the smallest speck of dust in the eye.
corruption_paragraphs: The honest hazard is a homophone. Mote and moat sound alike, and the word mote has all but vanished from daily speech, so a modern hearer may momentarily furnish his brother’s eye with a ditch of water instead of a fleck of dust. The image the Lord built is exact and must be kept: the mote is the very smallest thing, deliberately chosen against the beam to make the hypocrisy absurd. Lose the smallness of the mote and you blunt the whole rebuke, for the sting lies in a man magnifying a speck while carrying a log.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond the fading of the word itself. The principle to recover is the God-ward order of correction. Our age reads Mat 7 as though it forbade all judgment — “do not remove the mote at all” — but Christ commands the removal; He only commands it in the right order. First the beam, then the mote; first repentance, then reproof; first the searching of my own heart, then the help of my brother. The fault-finder sins not by seeing the speck but by seeing it before he sees his own timber, correcting from a proud height rather than a humbled one. True zeal for a brother’s holiness begins on one’s knees. The man who has cast the beam from his own eye does not stop caring about the mote; he now sees clearly enough to take it out gently, as one forgiven sinner serving another.
roots_summary: The word means the tiniest speck of dust or chaff in the eye — not a moat, and never a great fault.
roots_lines: Mote — from Old English mot, “a particle of dust.”
It is the smallest thing the eye can hold, chosen against the beam.
Christ set the mote against the beam to expose the hypocrite (Mat 7:3).
The censorious offer to remove a speck while blind with a plank (Mat 7:4).
Only the eye cleared of its beam can cast a brother’s mote (Mat 7:5).
usage: The KJV’s mote is a speck of dust in the eye, not a moat around a castle.
He beheld the mote in his brother’s eye and never felt the beam in his own.
First cast out the beam: only a healed eye can take the mote from another.

etymology: From Latin titulus, “a heading or superscription,” which came to mean a small mark written above a letter. In the KJV it is the tiniest stroke of the pen — the little horn or serif that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another.
biblical_def: A tittle in the Authorized Version is the smallest stroke of writing — the little projecting horn or serif that tells one Hebrew letter from its near twin. Paired with the jot, the least of the letters, it stands for the very last atom of Scripture. The Lord uses it to fence the enduring authority of God’s Word: “Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled” (Mat 5:18). Not a letter, not the horn of a letter, shall fall to the ground unaccomplished. Luke presses the same permanence: “it is easier for heaven and earth to pass, than one tittle of the law to fail” (Luk 16:17). Here is the doctrine the Reformed church calls verbal and plenary inspiration — that God breathed out not merely the ideas of Scripture but its very words, down to the least mark, so that “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable” (2Ti 3:16). The psalmist had sung the ground of it: “For ever, O LORD, thy word is settled in heaven” (Psa 119:89) — fixed above the reach of change. If the smallest stroke of the Law is unbreakable, then no promise is too small to trust and no command too slight to keep. The God who will not let a tittle fail will not fail His people; every jot of His Word shall stand when the heavens are rolled up as a scroll.
webster_summary: The smallest stroke or point of a written letter; a mark standing for the least part of Scripture.

corruption_summary: The idiom “jot and tittle” survives, but few now know a tittle is the least stroke of a letter — and the doctrine it teaches.
corruption_paragraphs: The honest drift is that the word has become a fossil inside a phrase. People still say “every jot and tittle” to mean “every last detail,” but scarcely one in a hundred could say what a tittle is: the little horn on a Hebrew letter, the hair’s-breadth stroke that keeps one letter from being read as another. Recovering the picture recovers the point. The Lord did not say that the great themes of the Law would stand; He said the smallest pen-stroke would stand, and that is a claim about the words of Scripture, not merely its ideas.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word, yet the doctrine it carries is under steady assault. Much modern religion prizes the “spirit” of Scripture while loosening its letter, treating the words as a husk around a timeless kernel that each age may reshape. The tittle forbids this. If not one stroke of the Law shall fail (Luk 16:17), then the words themselves are the breath of God, verbally and fully inspired, “given by inspiration of God, and… profitable” in all their parts (2Ti 3:16). This is why the Reformed church contends for the very text, why translation is done with fear, and why the least command binds. The word is “settled in heaven” (Psa 119:89), above the vote of scholars and the fashion of ages. A God who guards every tittle will keep every promise; the smallness of the stroke is the measure of His faithfulness.
roots_summary: The word means the smallest stroke of a written letter — a witness to the verbal inspiration of every word of Scripture.

etymology: From the Old French frenge, from Late Latin fimbria, “a border or fringe.” In the KJV it renders the Hebrew tzitzit, the twisted tassel commanded on the corners of the garment — not a decorative edge but a memorial appointed by God.
biblical_def: A fringe in the Authorized Version is the tassel — the tzitzit — that the LORD commanded Israel to wear on the corners of the garment as a standing memorial of His commandments. It is not, as the modern ear supposes, a mere ornamental border or a decorative trim; it is a preaching thread, appointed to catch the eye and turn the heart. The LORD is exact about both its making and its meaning. “Bid them that they make them fringes in the borders of their garments throughout their generations, and that they put upon the fringe of the borders a ribband of blue” (Num 15:38). The blue thread lifted the eye heavenward. And the purpose follows plainly: “that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD, and do them; and that ye seek not after your own heart and your own eyes, after which ye use to go a whoring” (Num 15:39). The tassel was an outward help against an inward wandering — a thing seen, set against the roving of the heart and the eyes. Moses repeats the charge in Deuteronomy: “Thou shalt make thee fringes upon the four quarters of thy vesture” (Deu 22:12). So the godly Israelite carried the Law woven at his hem, that a glance downward might recall him from sin to obedience. The fringe preached; the question was always whether the wearer would remember, or merely be seen wearing it.
webster_summary: The commanded tassel on the corners of the Israelite’s garment, worn as a memorial of God’s law.
webster_full: FRINGE, an ornamental border of threads or tassels; in Scripture, the appointed tassel on the garment’s corners.

corruption_summary: The modern ear hears “fringe” as a decorative trim or the far edge of a thing; the AV means a God-commanded memorial tassel.
corruption_paragraphs: The honest drift has carried the word two ways, both misleading. To the modern ear a fringe is either a bit of decorative trim on a curtain or lampshade, or else the outer margin of a thing — the “fringe” of a crowd, the “lunatic fringe” of a movement. Neither catches what the LORD commanded. The biblical fringe was not ornament and not margin; it was a memorial, a divinely appointed tassel with a thread of blue, meant to be looked at and obeyed. It sat at the edge of the garment, but it stood at the center of a duty: to remember the commandments and do them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond that softening into mere decoration. The principle to recover is God’s kindness in giving His people outward helps against inward drift. The fringe was a mercy to weak memories: a thing seen, set against “your own heart and your own eyes, after which ye use to go a whoring” (Num 15:39). The LORD knew the roving eye and the wandering heart, and appointed a visible sign to recall His people to obedience. Under the new covenant the tassel is gone, but the principle abides in the ordinances Christ has given His church — the Word read and preached, the water, the bread and cup — outward and visible helps that catch the eye and turn the heart to remember. The danger, then as now, was to wear the sign and forget the substance, to keep the tassel and lose the LORD; but rightly used, the fringe preached obedience at every glance.

etymology: Hem is from Old English hemm, “a border or edge.” In the Gospels it renders the Greek kraspedon, the tasseled border of the outer garment — the same fringed corner the Law commanded — not a plain sewn edge.
biblical_def: The hem of the garment in the Authorized Version is the tasseled border of the outer robe — the very fringe the Law commanded, worn at the corner where it could be reached and touched. The modern ear hears hem and pictures a plain stitched edge, but the Greek names the tassel; and it is this the diseased and desperate reached for in Christ. “A woman, which was diseased with an issue of blood twelve years, came behind him, and touched the hem of his garment” (Mat 9:20), and was made whole — not by the cloth but by the faith that pressed through the crowd to Him. Wherever He went the sick besought Him “that they might only touch the hem of his garment: and as many as touched were made perfectly whole” (Mat 14:36); at every village they reached for “the border of his garment” and were healed (Mar 6:56). Luke tells the woman’s story: she “touched the border of his garment: and immediately her issue of blood stanched” (Luk 8:44). The lesson is not that the hem held magic. Christ turned and asked who touched Him, and named the true channel: “thy faith hath made thee whole.” The tassel that Israel wore to remember the commandments now hung on the incarnate Lawgiver Himself, and the faith that laid hold of even its edge laid hold of Him. Virtue flowed from the Person, along the thread of faith, to the trembling hand at His hem.
webster_summary: The tasseled border of Christ’s outer robe, touched in faith by the sick and made whole.
webster_full: HEM OF THE GARMENT, the border or tasseled edge of the outer robe, especially that of Christ, touched for healing.

corruption_summary: The modern ear hears “hem” as a plain sewn edge; the Gospels mean the tasseled fringe of the Law, touched in faith.
corruption_paragraphs: The honest drift is a loss of the tassel. Say “hem” today and one thinks of the folded, stitched bottom edge of a garment — a matter for the tailor, nothing more. But the word in the Gospels is the fringe, the tzitzit the Law commanded on the corners of the robe (Num 15:38), and it hung loose enough to be reached from behind in a crowd. Restoring the picture restores the poignancy: the woman did not clutch at a stitched seam but at the memorial-tassel of the commandments, worn now by the One who gave them. She laid hold of the Law made flesh at the very thread that preached obedience.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond that shrinking of the word to a tailor’s edge. The principle to recover is that healing virtue lay never in the cloth but in Christ, and reached the sufferer along the line of faith. Superstition would make the hem a relic, a charmed object whose mere fabric heals; and much false religion has done just that with threads and bones and shrines. Scripture forbids it. The Lord felt virtue go out of Him and sought the woman not to praise her boldness but to name her faith: it was that, not the tassel, that made her whole. So the reaching hand is a parable of saving faith itself — weak, trembling, coming from behind, laying hold of the least edge of Christ, and finding the whole of Him. As many as touched Him in faith were made perfectly whole (Mat 14:36); the hem was only where the faith took hold.
roots_summary: The word means the tasseled border of Christ’s robe, touched in faith — not a plain stitched edge.

etymology: Border is from the Old French bordure, “an edge.” In the Gospels it names the tasseled corners of the robe — the commanded fringes — which the Pharisees enlarged; the same borders Israel was to make in Num 15:38, here swollen for display.
biblical_def: The borders of their garments in the Authorized Version are the tasseled corners of the robe — the commanded fringes — which the Pharisees deliberately made larger to be admired. The border itself was holy: the LORD had bid Israel “make them fringes in the borders of their garments… and that they put upon the fringe of the borders a ribband of blue” (Num 15:38). The sin was not in wearing it but in swelling it for show. The Lord names the motive with terrible plainness: “all their works they do for to be seen of men: they make broad their phylacteries, and enlarge the borders of their garments” (Mat 23:5). A memorial meant to turn the wearer’s own heart to obedience had been enlarged to turn other men’s eyes to the wearer. It is the exact vice the Sermon on the Mount forbids: “Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven” (Mat 6:1). The same men “desire to walk in long robes, and love greetings in the markets, and the highest seats in the synagogues” (Luk 20:46) — piety fashioned into a costume. The broad border is hypocrisy made visible: the tassel that once preached “remember the commandments” now preached “behold the man who wears it.” God looks past the widened fringe to the narrowed heart, and the applause of men is the only reward such devotion will ever receive.
webster_summary: The tasseled fringes of the robe, enlarged by the Pharisees to be seen of men — piety turned to display.

Beware of the scribes, which desire to walk in long robes, and love greetings in the markets, and the highest seats in the synagogues, and the chief rooms at feasts;
corruption_summary: A God-given memorial turned into a costume of self-display — and the same show-piety thrives wherever devotion is performed for an audience.
corruption_paragraphs: Here the honest drift of the word meets a live and perennial sin. To the modern ear a “border” is any decorative edge, and the force of Christ’s rebuke is easily lost; but the picture is precise. The Pharisees took the commanded fringe — a private aid to their own remembrance — and made it broad, so that the badge of humble obedience became a placard of superior holiness. This is not a museum sin. It walks into every age dressed for the times: the loud tithe, the conspicuous fast, the strategically public prayer, and in our own day the devotion staged for a camera and the good deed announced to an audience of followers. The tassel has changed; the enlargement has not.

The principle to recover is that God weighs the motive beneath the show. “All their works they do for to be seen of men” (Mat 23:5) — and being seen of men is the whole of their wage, for they “have no reward of your Father which is in heaven” (Mat 6:1). The broad border reveals the narrow heart: religion arranged for spectators, holiness worn like a long robe for the greetings it draws in the markets (Luk 20:46). The remedy is not to strip off the fringe but to shrink the self — to do alms in secret, to pray to the Father who sees in secret, to let the left hand not know what the right hand does. True piety wears its obedience where God can see it and does not care whether men can. The moment devotion begins to perform, it has already received its reward, and it is a poor and passing one: the applause of the very men it was staged for.
